items.prompt: Ben runs five days a week, all at an easy pace, to get faster. What is wrong with the plan?
choices: It adds effort with no aim at the speed gap
It leaves him too few rest days in each week
It makes every run far too long for his legs
items.explanation: Easy kilometres rehearse a pace he already has. The goal needs speed, so the effort is real but unaimed.

items.prompt: What does a promotion committee mainly look for?
choices: The total number of hours worked all year
Specific proof of work at the next level
How busy the person looked in every week
items.explanation: A committee judges proof against the bar. Hours and busyness are at most a side signal.

items.prompt: Jordan worked overtime for six months and was turned down. What best explains it?
choices: Overtime is never counted toward any promotion
The committee dislikes people who work late hours
The overtime did not target the gap being judged
items.explanation: Overtime is real work, but if none of it touched the skill being judged, it produced nothing the committee could score.

items.prompt: Which is evidence of readiness?
choices: A shipped project showing the missing skill
A calendar packed with long weekly meetings
A long list of tasks started this quarter
items.explanation: Evidence is something visible that shows the required ability. Meetings and started tasks show activity, not ability.

items.prompt: Effort on its own is best described as what?
choices: A direction with no set amount at all
An amount with no built-in direction
Proof that a gap has been closed out
items.explanation: Effort says how much, never where. Direction comes from naming the gap.

items.prompt: Two people work the same hours. What decides whose evidence is stronger?
choices: Whose desk sits nearer to the manager
Who logs the most hours in the last week
Whether the work targeted what is judged
items.explanation: The hours are equal, so what separates them is whether the work targeted the thing being judged.

items.prompt: Which plan has a direction?
choices: Close one named gap using one chosen task
Do more of everything and hope it adds up
Stay visible and take whatever work appears
items.explanation: A plan needs a direction: a named gap and a chosen task aimed at it. The other two plans are amounts of activity.

items.prompt: Hard work that never touches the bar produces what?
choices: Strong evidence once enough hours have passed
Real output, yet no evidence aimed at the bar
A guaranteed place at the next calibration
items.explanation: Output exists, but none of it answers the judge's question, so it adds little useful evidence.

items.prompt: Rae and Tom each spent a year on stretch work. All of Rae's tasks built the skill the bar was missing; Tom's were varied and impressive but off target. What is most likely at review?
choices: Rae has evidence the committee can score; Tom has little of it
Both have equal evidence, since their hours worked were similar
Tom has stronger evidence, because his work was more varied
Neither has evidence, since only manager opinions are counted
items.explanation: Both worked a year, but only Rae's work lines up with the missing skill, so only Rae has proof to score. Variety and impressiveness do not substitute for relevance.
items.reference:
Effort vs. evidence
effort: hours, kilometres, tasks
evidence: proof the judge can score
same hours, different aim, different result
Why: a judge scores proof against the bar, not the amount of work behind it.
items.learnMore:
Effort vs. evidence

Effort is an amount; evidence is a visible example of the required ability. Only work aimed at the bar produces the second kind.

Common mistake

Assuming that more hours on anything will eventually add up to readiness.
items.reflection: Think of a goal you worked hard on and still missed. Was the work aimed at what was actually being judged?

items.prompt: A runner doubles weekly distance, all at an easy pace, to reach a faster 10 km goal. Which diagnosis is most accurate?
choices: Doubling distance always raises race pace within a month
The distance trains endurance but not speed asked
The easy pace is the only part of the plan that fails
Distance and speed are the same skill, so the plan works
items.explanation: Easy distance builds endurance, which the 10 km goal already has. The missing ingredient is speed, so more of the same does not touch the gap.

items.prompt: Jordan says: 'I put in more hours than anyone, so I have earned it.' Which reply best reflects how the decision works?
choices: Hours are the main input, so the committee made an error
Hours count only when they are worked in evenings or weekends
Hours show commitment, but the decision checks proof of skill
The decision ignores effort entirely, so working less is wise
items.explanation: Commitment is visible and appreciated, but the decision asks whether the specific next-level skill has been shown. Hours alone cannot answer that.

items.prompt: A skill gap is best described as what?
choices: How tired you feel when comparing yourself
A rating the manager hands out at year end
The missing proof between now and the bar
items.explanation: A gap is the specific missing proof between your current evidence and what the goal requires, not a mood.

items.prompt: Maya runs 6:30 per km and needs 5:30. What is her gap?
choices: One minute per kilometre of speed
Ten more kilometres of total distance
Five extra training days each week
items.explanation: 6:30 against 5:30 per km is one minute per kilometre. Her distance is already fine, so the gap is speed.

items.prompt: What is the first step of a skill gap analysis?
choices: Pick the most impressive project available now
Compare what you can show with what the bar needs
Ask for a much bigger workload right away
items.explanation: The analysis starts by comparing: list what the bar needs and what you can already show.

items.prompt: In Alex's table, which row was the real gap?
choices: Making sound decisions inside the own team
Staying reliable during on-call incidents
Leading a decision that spans several teams
items.explanation: Alex's own-team decisions and on-call work were strong. The unproven row was leading across teams.

items.prompt: A row marked 'no gap' means what?
choices: Evidence for that expectation already exists
That expectation never applies at the level
The person should stop doing that kind of work
items.explanation: No gap means proof exists. It does not mean the expectation is irrelevant or the work should stop.

items.prompt: Which statement names a gap?
choices: Not feeling ready for the next level at all
No example yet of leading a cross-team decision
Needing to become more of a leader somehow
items.explanation: A gap statement names a concrete missing example. The other two are feelings you cannot aim at.

items.prompt: Why compare row by row, not by overall impression?
choices: It makes the comparison look more official
It lets every single row count as the gap
It shows which expectation is unproven
items.explanation: Row by row shows which specific expectation lacks proof. An overall impression hides that.

items.prompt: A 'partial gap' means what?
choices: Some proof exists but it is weak or unstructured
No proof exists for that expectation at all
The expectation was removed from the bar
items.explanation: Partial means some proof exists but is thin. It is not zero proof and not a removed expectation.

items.prompt: Alex's table: own-team decisions strong, incident work strong, cross-team leadership no example, mentoring informal only. Which reading is correct?
choices: Mentoring is the main gap, because it is weakest overall
All four rows are gaps, since none is perfect for sure
There is no gap at all, because two rows are strong
Cross-team leadership is the main gap; mentoring partial
items.explanation: Cross-team leadership has no example at all, so it is the main gap. Mentoring has some informal proof, which makes it partial.
items.reference:
Skill gap analysis
row by row: expectation vs. what you can show
none / partial / real gap
name it, don't feel it
Why: a named gap tells you where to aim; a vague feeling of being unready does not.
items.learnMore:
Skill gap analysis

Compare each expectation of the goal with what you can currently demonstrate. Most rows need nothing; one or two need work, and those become the plan.

Common mistake

Treating 'not ready yet' as a gap, when it names nothing you can aim at.
items.reflection: Pick a goal you have. Write one row-by-row table of what it needs and what you can show now. Which row is the real gap?

items.prompt: A runner needs 5:30 per km and ran 6:30 on a test. Which statement keeps the gap and the plan separate?
choices: The gap is the weekly distance; the plan is running faster
The gap is one minute per km; the plan is work aimed at it
The gap is her motivation; the plan is a longer schedule
The gap and the plan are the same thing, said twice
items.explanation: The gap is the measured difference between where she is and where the goal is. The plan is the work chosen to close it, so they are two different things.

items.prompt: Which sentence is a gap statement rather than a feeling?
choices: I just do not feel quite ready for the next step yet
I think I should probably become better at most things
I have no example of leading a decision with two teams
I am worried that others are ahead of me right now
items.explanation: A gap statement points at a missing, checkable example. The others describe worry or general self-improvement that nobody could aim at.

items.prompt: What is the first step in the growth-plan loop?
choices: Pick a busy project
Name the gap
Ask for more hours
items.explanation: Everything else in the loop is aimed at a gap, so naming it comes first.

items.prompt: What comes right after designing one deliberate opportunity?
choices: Presenting the finished result for promotion
Waiting for the next review cycle to arrive
Doing the work and producing visible evidence
items.explanation: After designing the opportunity, you do the work and keep visible evidence. Presenting comes after the check-back.

items.prompt: The check-back step asks what?
choices: Does this evidence actually close the gap
Did I work more hours during this month
Is the project big enough to impress them
items.explanation: The check-back question is whether the evidence closes the gap, not how long or how large the effort was.

items.prompt: If the check-back says 'not yet', what happens next?
choices: Stop and wait for a whole year to pass
Go back and design a better-aimed opportunity
Announce the gap as closed all the same
items.explanation: A 'not yet' sends you back to step 2 to aim better. Waiting or declaring victory skips the point.

items.prompt: Why does the loop include a check-back step?
choices: It adds one more required weekly meeting
It replaces the need for any evidence at all
It keeps effort from drifting into busywork
items.explanation: Without a check, weeks of effort can drift into busywork. The check keeps the work aimed at the gap.

items.prompt: How many gaps should one pass of the loop target?
choices: One or two named gaps
Every skill you could ever improve
None until the review arrives
items.explanation: One or two gaps keep the plan focused. A list of everything dilutes the aim.

items.prompt: A music student needs smoother tempo changes. What is step 2?
choices: Play every familiar piece twice each single day
Choose a piece with tempo changes to practise
Buy a more expensive instrument before starting
items.explanation: Step 2 designs work that forces the missing skill, so a piece with tempo changes fits.

items.prompt: What lets you leave the loop?
choices: The calendar reaching the end of the month
Feeling tired of working on that one gap
Evidence that closes the gap, ready to show
items.explanation: You leave the loop once the evidence closes the gap and can be shown. Time passing or tiredness is not evidence.

items.prompt: Dana's check-back shows her first project proved the skill inside one team, but the gap names three teams. What should she do?
choices: Present the result, since a project was finished
Drop the gap, since effort was already spent here
Wait a full cycle and hope that the gap changes
Design a second opportunity that reaches scope
items.explanation: Her check-back found the evidence covered one team while the gap names three. Going back to step 2 with a better-aimed opportunity is what the loop prescribes.
items.reference:
The growth-plan loop
1. name the gap
2. design one opportunity
3. do it, keep the evidence
4. check back; loop if not yet
Why: the check-back step is what keeps effort aimed at the gap instead of drifting.
items.learnMore:
The growth-plan loop

Name the gap, design one deliberate opportunity, produce visible evidence, then check whether it closes the gap. If not, go back and aim better.

Common mistake

Skipping the check-back and assuming finished work means the gap is closed.
items.reflection: Think of something you practised for weeks. When did you last check whether it was closing the gap you cared about?

items.prompt: A friend calls the loop 'just a to-do list'. What distinguishes it?
choices: The check-back tests whether evidence closes the gap
It contains more steps than an ordinary to-do list does
It forces every task to be finished strictly in order
It is designed so that no step is ever repeated twice
items.explanation: A to-do list tracks completion. The loop's check-back tests whether what was completed actually closed the gap, and sends you back if not.

items.prompt: Which order is the loop in?
choices: Produce evidence, name the gap, check back, design an opportunity
Design an opportunity, check back, name the gap, produce evidence
Name the gap, design an opportunity, produce evidence, check back
Check back, produce evidence, design an opportunity, name the gap
items.explanation: The order is name, design, produce, check. Naming first is what gives every later step something to aim at.

items.prompt: Why ask the judge what the bar is?
choices: The standard often exists only in their head
Asking is always faster than any other work
Guessing is never allowed at any workplace
items.explanation: Expectations at a level are often unwritten and live with the judge, so asking beats guessing.

items.prompt: A calibration conversation means what?
choices: Negotiating a raise before showing evidence
Asking the judge what would prove readiness
Comparing your hours with a teammate's hours
items.explanation: A calibration conversation asks the judge what proof would show readiness.

items.prompt: Which is a good calibration question?
choices: Do you think I am doing a good job overall at this?
Will I be promoted if I just keep working hard?
What one or two things stand between me and the next level?
items.explanation: It asks for a concrete answer about the gap. The others invite a vague opinion or a promise nobody can make.

items.prompt: The same job title can mean what across teams?
choices: Different specific expectations
Exactly identical expectations everywhere
No expectations of any kind
items.explanation: Titles carry different expectations on different teams, which is another reason to ask.

items.prompt: A piano student asks the teacher what the exam piece demands. What is this?
choices: A way of avoiding practice
A calibration conversation
A guess at the bar
items.explanation: The teacher holds the marking sheet. Asking what the piece demands is exactly a calibration conversation.

items.prompt: There is no manager to ask. Where can the bar come from?
choices: Whatever feels most impressive right now to you
Nowhere, so the goal cannot really be planned
A rubric, a peer, or a hiring manager's brief
items.explanation: With no manager, use the most credible source of the standard, such as a rubric or a peer at that level.

items.prompt: Honest self-assessment alone can still miss what?
choices: Which weakness is blocking the decision
Every weakness you personally have in total
The number of hours you worked all year
items.explanation: You can be accurate about yourself and still pick the wrong weakness, because the bar sits with the judge.

items.prompt: After the conversation, the gap should be what?
choices: A vague sense to be revisited
A concrete target that is named
A matter settled forever for all
items.explanation: The point of asking is a concrete, nameable target that you can then revisit as things change.

items.prompt: Two colleagues are candid about their weaknesses. One guesses 'public speaking' while the committee wants cross-team leadership. What does this show?
choices: Candid people never choose the wrong gap by mistake
Public speaking is never relevant at any level
The committee should have told them nothing at all
Honest self-assessment can still aim at wrong gaps
items.explanation: Candour about yourself does not reveal what the committee weighs. Honest self-review can still point at the wrong gap, which is why you ask.
items.reference:
Asking instead of guessing
the bar lives in the judge's head
self-review accurate, target still wrong
ask: what proof would you need?
Why: an honest list of your weaknesses can still miss the one that blocks the decision.
items.learnMore:
Asking instead of guessing

A calibration conversation asks the judge what proof would show readiness. If there is no clear judge, use the most credible written or human source of the standard.

Common mistake

Choosing a gap by self-assessment alone and never confirming it with whoever decides.
items.reflection: Where in your life does someone else hold the marking sheet? Have you asked what is on it?

items.prompt: Which opening gets the most usable answer in a calibration conversation?
choices: What proof would you need to see from me next level?
Am I on track to be promoted this year or not?
Can you tell me how my peers are doing right now?
Do you think I should simply work harder this period?
items.explanation: This question asks for specific proof tied to the next level. The others ask for reassurance, comparison with peers, or a vague instruction.

choices: Skip the standard and pick whatever seems the hardest
Find the most credible source of the standard
Wait until a judge appears without being asked at all
Use total hours worked as the standard of success
items.explanation: Without a named judge, the nearest equivalent is a credible source of the standard. Hours or whatever feels hard are not a standard.

items.prompt: Alex's gap is leading a decision across teams. Which project fits?
choices: A large project inside Alex's own team group
A solo side project done on quiet weekends
A migration spanning two teams, led by Alex
items.explanation: A two-team migration structurally requires cross-team leadership, so it produces exactly the missing proof.

items.prompt: Why would a big same-team project not close Alex's gap?
choices: It never exercises cross-team leadership
Big projects are never counted at all by anyone
Same-team projects are always much too easy
items.explanation: Same-team work never puts the cross-team skill to use, no matter how big it is.

items.prompt: Which evidence did Alex's migration produce?
choices: A record number of overtime hours
A written RFC and a shipped result
A list of tasks assigned to others
items.explanation: The RFC and the shipped result are checkable proof of leading a cross-team decision. Hours and task lists are not.

items.prompt: In the toy model, what does one targeted opportunity give?
choices: 100 out of 100
35 out of 100
70 out of 100
items.explanation: In the toy model, one opportunity gives 70 points of evidence strength.

items.prompt: In the toy model, how many opportunities reach 100?
choices: Two
One
Zero
items.explanation: Two opportunities give 140, which is capped at 100, so two reach the top.

items.prompt: In the toy model, a third opportunity for the same gap adds what?
choices: Another 70 points above the cap, in full
Nothing, since the score is already capped
A penalty for doing too much of the work
items.explanation: Once the score is capped at 100, another opportunity for the same gap adds nothing in this toy model.

items.prompt: A study group where a student teaches one topic weekly builds which two skills?
choices: Memorising facts and fast typing
Neither one, since it is only social
Leadership and clearer explanation
items.explanation: Leading the group builds leadership and teaching builds clear explanation, so one activity serves both gaps.

items.prompt: If a manager names two gaps, one well-designed opportunity may do what?
choices: Produce evidence for both gaps
Always need two entirely separate projects
Safely ignore the second gap
items.explanation: A well-designed opportunity can serve more than one gap. It does not have to be a separate project each time.

items.prompt: Alex's manager names two gaps: cross-team leadership and structured mentoring. Which design is strongest?
choices: Lead two unrelated projects, each only half as long
Lead the migration and ignore mentoring until later on
Mentor three people on tasks inside the own team
Lead the migration; let a newer teammate own a piece
items.explanation: The migration covers cross-team leadership and the teammate owning a piece covers mentoring, so one design serves both gaps. The other options leave one gap untouched or split the effort thin.
items.reference:
Targeted opportunity
gap: lead a decision across teams
fits: a two-team migration led by Alex
misses: a big project inside one team
Why: relevance to the named gap matters more than the size or visibility of the project.
items.learnMore:
Targeted opportunity

Choose work that structurally forces the missing skill to be used. One well-designed opportunity can sometimes produce evidence for two gaps.

Common mistake

Picking a large, visible project that never exercises the skill being judged.
items.reflection: What is one piece of work you could take that would force the skill you lack, rather than merely look impressive?

items.prompt: In the toy model, someone takes a third opportunity after two. What is the right reading?
choices: The score stays at 100; effort is better spent elsewhere
The score rises to 140, which proves extra readiness
The score drops, since too many projects lowers quality
The score doubles, as the third one counts for double
items.explanation: In the toy model the score is capped at 100, so a third opportunity at the same gap adds nothing. Spending it on another gap is the better move.

items.prompt: Which opportunity best matches the gap 'no evidence of owning a rollout end to end'?
choices: Write design documents for rollouts led by other people
Lead a rollout from plan to finish and record results
Attend every rollout review meeting held this quarter
Fix many small bugs found after other people's rollouts
items.explanation: Leading a rollout end to end is the exact missing capability. The others support rollouts without owning one.

items.prompt: After closing the gap, what must Alex do?
choices: Wait quietly for it to be noticed there
Bring the evidence to the calibration talk
Start over with an unrelated new goal
items.explanation: Evidence has to reach the judge. The calibration conversation is where it is weighed.

items.prompt: Evidence that exists but is never shown does what?
choices: Counts automatically anyway
Counts double the following year
Cannot influence the decision
items.explanation: Hidden evidence cannot affect a decision the judge makes without it.

items.prompt: Which package did Alex bring in month six?
choices: The RFC, the resolved disagreement and the result
A summary of the hours spent across six months
A list of the teams that showed some interest
items.explanation: Alex brought the specific evidence: the written proposal, the resolved disagreement and the result.

items.prompt: Gaps and expectations can do what over time?
choices: Never change once they have been named at all
Shift, so the plan is revisited at calibrations
Disappear whenever the person gets quite busy
items.explanation: Bars and gaps can move, so the plan is revisited at each calibration.

items.prompt: A gap was guessed and never confirmed. What is the risk?
choices: The plan becomes much too short to follow
The judge receives far too much evidence
Effort goes to a gap that is not the blocker
items.explanation: A guessed gap may not be the blocker, so the work may be aimed at the wrong target.

items.prompt: A runner reports a new time-trial result to the coach. What does this match?
choices: Bringing evidence back to the judge
Telling friends how hard they trained
Resting until race day with no data
items.explanation: The coach is the judge, and the time trial is the evidence, so reporting it matches Alex bringing evidence back.

items.prompt: Why revisit the plan at each calibration?
choices: Plans expire after exactly six months of use
The bar or the person's gaps may have changed
Evaluators dislike any kind of long-term plan
items.explanation: Things change between calibrations, so the plan has to be rechecked against the current bar.

items.prompt: Alex's case is best treated as what?
choices: A script every person must copy exactly
A rule that applies to library migrations only
One worked example, not the whole territory
items.explanation: Alex's story is one case. The shape transfers, but details have to be re-derived.

items.prompt: Casey closes the named gap with a strong result but tells no one, and the review passes without it. What failed?
choices: The gap was guessed instead of asked about at all
The opportunity was too small for the bar to count
The evidence existed but was not shown to the judge
The check-back step was run far too often to matter
items.explanation: The work was done but never shown, so it could not weigh in. The gap itself was fine and the check-back was not the problem.
items.reference:
Surfacing evidence and revisiting
bring specific evidence, not effort
ask: does this close the gap?
expect the gap to shift
Why: evidence the judge never sees cannot change the decision, and gaps can move.
items.learnMore:
Surfacing evidence and revisiting

Show the evidence, ask whether it closes the gap, and treat a changed answer as a new pass of the loop. Alex's case is one example, not the whole territory.

Common mistake

Closing the gap quietly and assuming the evaluator will notice on their own.
items.reflection: Change one detail of Alex's story: a worse deadline, a different audience. Which step of the loop is under the most pressure?

items.prompt: At the next calibration the manager names a different gap. What is the best response?
choices: Treat it as a new pass: name it, design, then prove it
Argue that the first gap should still decide everything
Repeat the first opportunity with an even higher profile
Decide the evaluator is unreliable and stop all planning
items.explanation: A new gap is a new run of the same loop. Ignoring it or giving up on planning drops the lesson.
items.reference:
Surfacing evidence and revisiting
bring specific evidence, not effort
ask: does this close the gap?
expect the gap to shift
Why: evidence the judge never sees cannot change the decision, and gaps can move.
items.learnMore:
Surfacing evidence and revisiting

Show the evidence, ask whether it closes the gap, and treat a changed answer as a new pass of the loop. Alex's case is one example, not the whole territory.

items.prompt: Which case uses Alex's pattern well outside promotions, with a different audience?
choices: A student studies longer hours and simply hopes the teacher notices it
A student asked to explain better leads a study group and shares notes
A student guesses the weak area and avoids asking the teacher about it
A student takes more classes that have no link to any feedback at all
items.explanation: Leading a study group and sharing notes is the same shape: a named gap, an aimed opportunity and evidence brought back, with a different audience.
